question: What does each of several factors do, and do they work together?

steps.title: Pick factors
steps.text: Name the things you can set (factors), and the settings of each (levels), such as on and off.

quotes.text: Each intervention and its comparator(s) together comprise a factor.
These levels are specific interventions and comparators within a factor.

steps.title: Cross them
steps.text: Cross every level of every factor: two factors with two levels give four combinations.

quotes.text: All factors and levels are combined so that the design comprises all possible combinations of factor levels, and all participants are eligible to be randomised for each factor.

steps.title: Randomise
steps.text: Chance assigns each unit (a person, a plot, a batch) to one combination, so every unit tests every factor at once.

quotes.text: A trial in which two or more interventions are assessed in the same participants.

steps.title: Main effects
steps.text: For factor A, compare everyone with A on against everyone with A off, whatever B was; then do the same for B. Each unit is used twice, which is where the economy comes from.

quotes.text: All participants allocated to active A are compared against all those allocated to control A, and similarly for the factor B comparison.
Complete and fractional factorial designs and single-factor designs are generally more economical than conducting individual experiments on each factor.

steps.title: Interaction
steps.text: If A's effect changes when B is on, the factors interact, and A's average effect describes neither case. Check for it.

quotes.text: Occurs when the effect of one intervention depends on whether participants also receive the other intervention.
If treatments interact, then the assumptions underpinning the 2-in-1 trial motivation are no longer valid.

steps.title: Fewer runs
steps.text: With many factors, run a chosen fraction of the combinations; you give up some interactions to keep the main effects.

quotes.text: Some combinations of factors are omitted.
fractional factorial designs merit serious consideration because of their economy and versatility.

forking-paths.text: evaluating multiple interactions increases the risk of false-positive findings, which can affect interpretation.

exercise.title: What the margins estimate
exercise.intro: A 2 × 2 experiment. Set what A and B really do, and how much extra you get when both are on. Then read what each comparison of the four cells tells you about A.

quote.text: Trials in which the factorial design has been chosen for efficiency (2-in-1 trials) rely on the assumption that treatments work independently, meaning that the effect of one intervention is assumed to be consistent in the presence or absence of other intervention(s).
